title: The What-If Scenario Lab
goal: Your kid takes a big what-if, like keeping only ten things, and thinks it all the way through. They map what would really happen, find someone who has lived something like it, make a plan, try a small slice of it for real, then take the plan back to someone who knows and find out what they missed.
need: Someone to ask who has lived something like it
A few hours to try a small slice for real
Books or the internet for looking things up (optional)

levelsLine: Every step has three levels: Explore, Develop, Extend. Pick the one that fits your kid today, and change it anytime. Siblings can do the same step at different levels, side by side.

howTo.intro: You don't need any expertise. Your job is to wonder alongside them, take every idea seriously and keep asking 'And then what?' Share what you'd worry about too. Then try a piece of it for real, because that's where the plan learns the most.

plan.what: Pick a what-if and map what would happen (Steps 1 and 2).
Ask someone who knows, then make the plan and try a slice (Steps 3 and 4).
Take the plan back to someone who knows (Step 5).

troubleshoot.a: Pick a playful one, like Ten things or Kids in charge. Finish by asking what might be better in that world.
Ask 'And then what?' three times in a row. Short answers usually get longer by the third one.
Great. Don't correct them. Ask 'How would that work on Day 3?' and let the plan test itself.

lesson.text: A good what-if answer doesn't stop at the first idea. It keeps going: and then what, and then what, and who does that affect?
lesson.before: If I could only keep ten things, I'd keep my toys.

model.line: No toothbrush, no jacket, no blanket.
Give up three toys for a toothbrush, a jacket and a blanket?
One day using only ten things. The cold walk was the hardest part.

lesson.modelNote: The first answer solved the first hour. The second kept going, ran into a hard choice and then got tested for real.

steps.title: Choose your what-if
steps.why: The best question is the one they can't stop thinking about.
steps.kid: Your kid picks a question from the What-ifs card in the Scenario Toolkit at the end of the guide, or invents their own. Then they say what would make it hard, not just different.
steps.you: Pick one too and say what would bother you most. Then help them choose the one they're most curious about.
ask: What would you miss the most?
What might be better in that world?
steps.tip: Pick the one they keep arguing about. Arguing means they care.

levels.explore: Pick one what-if and say or draw what you'd do first.
levels.develop: Pick two and name the biggest problem in each.
levels.extend: Invent your own what-if, and check it's hard enough to think about for a week.

steps.title: Map what would happen
steps.why: The first day is easy. Day 3 is where it gets interesting.
steps.kid: Your kid walks through it day by day, using the Keep asking card: what changes first, what gets harder by Day 3 and Day 7, who it's hardest for and what people would argue about. They add a line every time someone says 'And then what?'
steps.you: Ask about the things they haven't thought of yet, like the neighbours, the pets, the grandparents. Say 'Here's what I'd worry about' and add one of your own.
ask: What problem would show up that most people wouldn't think of?
Who would this be hardest for?
steps.tip: Draw three columns: Day 1, Day 3, Day 7. It's a lot easier to see the problems pile up.

levels.explore: Name three things that would change in the first week.
levels.develop: Map the problems across Day 1, Day 3 and Day 7.
levels.extend: Build a timeline with practical problems, feelings and who'd disagree about what.

steps.title: Ask someone who knows
steps.why: Somebody has already lived some version of this.
steps.kid: Your kid finds out how real people have handled something like it. Best of all, they ask someone, using the Ask them card: a grandparent who remembers a long power cut, a neighbour who grew up on a farm, a friend who moved countries. Then they write down what surprised them.
steps.you: Help them think of who to ask, and make the call or visit together. Look things up with them if there's no one to ask.
ask: What did they do that you wouldn't have thought of?
What was the hardest part for them?
steps.tip: A video call counts. Grandparents far away often love being asked.

levels.explore: Ask one person, or find one story, and share what you learned.
levels.develop: Ask one person and find two facts, and say how each changes your thinking.
levels.extend: Compare two real examples from different places, and work out why people handled them differently.

steps.title: Make the plan, then try a slice
steps.why: A plan on paper has never had to make supper.
steps.kid: Your kid writes what you'd do on Day 1, how you'd handle the biggest problems and what you'd have to give up. Then you all live a small slice from the Try a slice card for a few hours, and they fix the plan with what they learned.
steps.you: Ask 'What about...?' to find the gaps, and then really do the slice. No cheating, for the agreed time. Use flashlights rather than candles, and keep the safety rules you always have.
ask: If you can only keep one, which one?
steps.tip: Keep the slice short, and pick a real start and end time. A few hours is plenty to feel it.

levels.explore: Say three things you'd do first, and try the slice with your family.
levels.develop: Plan for each big problem, name a trade-off, try the slice and change one thing.
levels.extend: Plan for the first week, the first month and beyond, name three trade-offs, and use the slice to test your riskiest idea.

steps.title: Take it back to someone who knows
steps.why: The person who lived it will spot what you missed.
steps.kid: Your kid fills in Our plan at the end of the guide and takes it back to the person they asked in Step 3, or someone new who's lived it. They ask what's missing and add it. Then they put the final plan beside their Day 1 column and see how far it's come.
steps.you: Go with them. If the answer stings a bit, help them hear it as a good sign: it means the person took the plan seriously.
ask: What did they spot that you missed?
steps.tip: Ask 'What would you have needed that isn't here?' It's an easy question to answer honestly.

levels.explore: Show your plan to one person and add one thing they suggest.
levels.develop: Fill in Our plan, take it to someone who knows and change two things.
levels.extend: Ask two people who've lived it to check the plan, and decide what to do where they disagree.

conclusion.headline: They didn't stop at the first answer.
conclusion.text: Listen at supper. If they say 'But then what would happen?' about something in the news, a family plan or a story they're reading, the habit is sticking.
conclusion.celebrate: Put their Day 1 column beside the final plan and say: 'Look how far you took that.'
extensions: Pick a what-if about history, and find out what really happened

signs: They ask what happens next instead of stopping at the first answer
They try a small piece of something before deciding
They ask people who've lived it
makeItReal: Keep a running list of what-ifs on the fridge, and pull one out whenever someone says they're bored.
